If you're wondering...

Why is nature so productive?

A forest never gets a bag of artificial fertilizer, is never dug over, and yet it grows denser, richer, and more fertile year after year — for millions of years, without anyone maintaining it. Compare that to a farm field, which without annual fertilizing becomes exhausted within a few seasons, and the question forces itself on you: what does nature do that we don't do in our gardens?

Part of the answer lies in what the earlier reflections already touched on: diversity, layering, soil life allowed to do its work undisturbed. But there's a deeper difference, and it might be the most important one of all: in a natural ecosystem, nothing leaves the system. A leaf that falls decomposes right where it fell. An animal that dies is broken down on the spot and taken back up into the soil. Even what an animal eats largely returns to that same soil through its droppings. There's no truck that drives off with it in the evening.

That's exactly what makes a vegetable garden, however ecologically it's approached, structurally different. When you harvest a head of lettuce, bring in a bucket of carrots, or carry a basket of tomatoes indoors, you're taking away something your soil had built up — the minerals, the carbon, the biomass that were in that plant leave the system and don't come back on their own. Do that year after year without compensating for it, and you deplete your soil just as surely as a field that's never fertilized, even if you never dig and never use chemicals.

Realizing that harvesting is always a withdrawal is also the key to what a chaos garden can actually do: close the loop as much as possible instead of leaving it open. Mulch, compost, green manures, plant residue you leave lying instead of clearing away — each one is an attempt to give back what the harvest takes, so the system doesn't get depleted but keeps recovering. You'll never fully reach the level of a forest, since you're deliberately harvesting away what a forest simply leaves in place. But the more closely you manage to close that loop, the closer you get to the productivity nature sustains effortlessly.

Nature isn't productive because it gives nothing away — it's productive because nothing ever truly leaves. What you harvest, you have to give back yourself.
